turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?
turns.patient_response: Well, honestly, I'm mostly here because HR at my job and my sister keep saying I've gotten too thin. They've been on my case about it a lot lately. But from my side of things... I just see that my suits fit a lot sharper for work. My weight has just kept dropping since the divorce, and I guess it's making them nervous, so they pushed me to come in and talk to someone.

symptom_reasoning.S044: The patient reports continuous weight loss since their divorce, noting that family and workplace HR say they have gotten too thin.
symptom_reasoning.S084: The patient dismisses the concerns of HR and their sister regarding their low weight, viewing the weight drop positively as making work suits fit sharper.

turns.doctor_question: When your weight started dropping after the divorce, was that something you were actively trying to do, or did it happen without you really trying to lose weight?
turns.patient_response:
Well, at first I think I just wasn't eating much because of the stress. But after a while... yeah, I guess I started actively trying to keep the weight coming off. 

I keep a pretty tight lid on it now. Most days I just stick to coffee in the morning, and maybe I'll have a protein bar while I'm driving between sales calls. Then at night, I'll make something small, like just a piece of grilled chicken without any rice or anything heavy. It's just... I've found that once I sit down and eat a full meal, it feels like I completely messed up the whole day. So it's easier to just keep it strict.

symptom_reasoning.S043: The patient explicitly confirms restricting dietary intake by limiting daily food to coffee, a protein bar, and a small piece of chicken to keep weight off.

turns.doctor_question: After you eat, do you ever do anything to try to prevent the food from staying in your body—like making yourself throw up, using laxatives, or exercising intensely?
turns.patient_response:
No, I don't do any of that. I've never made myself throw up or taken laxatives or anything like that. And I don't really exercise all that much either, honestly—just normal walking around for my sales calls. 

Like I said, I just keep a really tight limit on what I eat in the first place, so I don't really have to worry about trying to get rid of it later. I just focus on keeping the intake low.

symptom_reasoning.S043: The patient confirms restrictive intake by stating they keep a tight limit on what they eat and focus on keeping their intake low.
symptom_reasoning.S047: The patient explicitly denies compensatory exercise, stating they do not exercise much beyond normal walking for work and do not try to get rid of food after eating.
symptom_reasoning.S048: The patient explicitly denies purging behaviors, stating they have never made themselves vomit or used laxatives.

turns.doctor_question: When you look at yourself in the mirror or think about your body right now, do you feel like you're overweight, or do you recognize that you're actually quite thin?
turns.patient_response:
Well, I wouldn't say I look at myself and think I'm massively overweight, but I definitely don't see what my sister sees. 

When I look in the mirror, especially before a big sales meeting or if I'm getting ready for a date, I just zero right in on my stomach and my face. If I think I look soft at all in those areas, I just... I feel like people are going to see me as sloppy or weak. So I guess I don't really see myself as "quite thin," because I'm still so focused on those soft spots.

symptom_reasoning.S046: The patient reports fixating on 'soft spots' on their stomach and face, not viewing themselves as thin, and linking these perceived flaws to being viewed as 'sloppy or weak,' reflecting distorted body image and undue influence of shape on self-evaluation.
